name: Convex hull formation
summary: Particles must enclose an object in its convex hull, sensing only locally.
statement: Particles must form the convex hull (and the weak $\mathcal{O}_\Delta$-hull) of a fixed object on the lattice. $B$ is the length of the object's boundary.

primer.intro: Imagine robots asked to seal an oddly shaped object inside the tightest convex 'fence', like a rubber band stretched around it. A fixed object occupies a connected set of nodes of the triangular grid, and particles sit next to it; $B$ is the length of the object's boundary. A particle sits on one node of an endless triangular grid and moves in two steps: it *expands* into an empty neighbouring node, briefly occupying both, then *contracts* into one of the two; so one expansion and one contraction move it by one node. The particles must occupy exactly the nodes of the object's *convex hull*, taken one layer outside the object: on the triangular grid, the smallest region bounded by six straight sides in the grid's three directions that contains the object. Particles have constant memory, no common compass, and an adversarial scheduler; one particle starts as a leader on the object's boundary. Time is counted in rounds (every particle acts at least once per round).

ideas.title: Walk around the object and push six walls outwards
ideas.idea:
1. Using its own compass, the leader names six directions and imagines six walls (half-planes), one per side of the future hull. It keeps six counters: its distance to each wall, all starting at 0.
2. The leader walks clockwise around the object's boundary. Each step brings it closer to two walls and farther from two others, and it updates the counters.
3. If a step would take it beyond a wall (a counter already at 0 must go down), that wall is *pushed* one step outwards: the estimate of the hull grows.
4. The leader also remembers, for each wall, whether it has touched that wall since its last push. Once it has touched all six without pushing any, the walls are in their final places.
5. The counters can be as large as $B$, too big for one particle, so the followers trailing the leader each store one bit of a binary counter.
6. Finally the particles fill the nodes along the six walls.
ideas.analysis: The walls only move outwards and stop at the true hull, so the walk ends with the correct hull. The paper proves that the whole process, including the distributed counters, takes $O(B)$ rounds [Daymude2020Hull]. The same algorithm can be extended to a tighter fence (the weak $\mathcal{O}_\Delta$-hull) in the same time; if there are too few particles, it forms as much of the hull as it can.
ideas.why_it_matters: Distributed binary counters let constant-memory particles count up to large numbers, a tool other algorithms reuse.

ideas.title: Someone must reach the far end
ideas.idea: This simple argument is ours; the catalogue records no lower bound for this problem. Let the object be a long straight bar, so $B$ is about twice its length, and let all the particles start bunched together near one end, enough of them to fill the hull. The hull has nodes next to the far end of the bar, at distance about $B/2$ from where the particles start, so some particle must travel about $B/2$ nodes.
ideas.analysis: Each node of travel takes one expansion and one contraction, and an unkind scheduler may let each particle act only once per round, so this takes at least about $B/2$ rounds. So $\Omega(B)$ rounds are needed in the worst case, and the $O(B)$ algorithm above is best possible on such inputs.
ideas.why_it_matters: It shows that the boundary length, not the number of particles, is the right measure for this problem.

history: Convex hull formation asked whether particles **without shared orientation** can compute a global geometric property, and how fast [Daymude2020Hull].

results.note: Introductory and current best; uses distributed binary counters.

figure.caption: Convex hull formation, following [Daymude2020Hull]: a leader (L) walks clockwise around the object (black) and keeps its distance to six walls, one per side of a hexagon with lattice-parallel sides; a step beyond a wall pushes that wall outwards (dashed: the current estimate). Here the particles already surround the object, so the leader advances by role swaps, handing its role and counters to the particle ahead, and nobody moves. Once the leader has touched all six walls since its last push, the hull is known, and the particle in the bay steps out (expansion, contraction), so that the particles occupy exactly the nodes adjacent to the hull.
